ABSTRACT
Accurate and efficient pixel-level crack detection is essential for infrastructure health monitoring. Although
recent encoder-decoder architectures have achieved notable results, their reliance on aggressive downsampling
often compromises the measurement-grade spatial precision required for fine crack detection. To address this
gap, we present HACNetV2, an enhanced full-resolution architecture that builds upon our previous HACNet.
Through key architectural refinements and novel components, HACNetV2 achieves substantially improved ef-
ficiency and effectiveness compared to its predecessor. HACNetV2 employs a dual-branch structure that in-
tegrates full-resolution and high-resolution processing to maintain critical spatial detail without imposing a
heavy computational burden. Additionally, we propose two novel components: the hybrid atrous spatial pyramid
attention module (HybridASPA), which expands the receptive field while reducing computational complexity,
and the crack-aware attention module (CrackAM), which enhances sensitivity to fine and complex crack features.
Together, these components enable HACNetV2 to enhance feature representation effectively. The experimental
results on the public BCL and CHCrack5K benchmark datasets demonstrate that HACNetV2 outperforms recent
models, achieving superior mIoU and F1 scores while maintaining a lightweight structure with only 0.52 M
parameters. Furthermore, HACNetV2 supports real-time inference capabilities, processing 480 × 480 images at
47 FPS on an RTX 3090 GPU.

This presents a critical challenge: how can full-resolution network be
accelerated while improving its performance across various crack
detection scenarios? In this study, we address this issue by building upon
HACNet as our baseline. Our preliminary experiments indicated that not
all crack features require computationally expensive full-resolution
convolution operations. To optimize this, we reduce the number of
channels in its high-resolution structure to lower computational costs. A
high-resolution branch at half the original image scale is then intro-
duced to enhance feature representation, thereby improving both the
accuracy and speed of crack detection. Additionally, recognizing the
success of attention mechanisms in computer vision, we revisited
existing channel attention mechanisms for crack detection. Our analysis
revealed that some attention mechanisms originally designed for natural
semantic scenes may be suboptimal for fine crack detection, which
aligns with earlier studies (Lan & Dong, 2022; Sun et al., 2024). In
natural semantic images, key features are densely distributed, allowing
attention mechanisms to focus on multiple regions with rich informa-
tion. In contrast, crack images typically contain sparse, elongated fea-
tures, with most of the image area being background. On the basis of
these observations, we propose a crack-aware attention module, named
CrackAM, to ensure that both fine and coarse cracks receive appropriate
attention. We also introduce the effective hybrid atrous spatial pyramid
attention (HybridASPA), which integrates CrackAM to enable efficient
multiscale feature aggregation. Our final built model, HACNetV2 (see
Fig. 1(c)), achieves an improved balance between accuracy and speed.

strike a balance between computational efficiency and segmen-

segmentation quality.

2. Related work
We briefly review existing model architectures relevant to our pro-
posed method.
2.1. Encoder-decoder networks for crack detection
Three classic encoder-decoder architectures—FCN (Long et al.
2015), U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015), and SegNet (Badrinarayanan
et al., 2017)—have demonstrated strong performance in pixel-level
crack detection (Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019). Subsequent
research has focused on enhancing these architectures. One approach
involves leveraging more powerful encoder backbones, including
ResNet variants (Bang et al., 2019) and Vision Transformers (ViT) (Liu
et al., 2023), to improve feature extraction capabilities. Another critical
strategy focuses on multi-scale feature fusion to capture contextual in-
formation across different resolutions. Techniques such as spatial pyr-
amid pooling (SPP) (Gu et al., 2023) and the explicit fusion of
hierarchical convolutional features (Wang and Su, 2022) are commonly
employed. For instance, Liu et al. (2019) proposed a DeepCrack network
adapting the FCN architecture with guided filters (He et al., 2013), while
Zou et al. (2018) introduced a distinct model, also termed DeepCrack,
built upon SegNet, which specifically fuses features from corresponding
encoder and decoder stages across scales.
The prediction speed is also critical for practical engineering appli-
cations in crack detection. Previous studies have focused on speeding up
encoder-decoder networks. For example, Chen et al. (2019) proposed a
learnable automatic switch module (SWM) that selectively bypasses the
decoder on the basis of the input image class, reducing computation by
31 %–87 % without sacrificing accuracy. Choi and Cha (2020) improved
the speed by replacing standard convolutions with separable convolu-
tions and using fewer channels. Li et al. (2023) introduced HrSegNet, a
real-time, high-resolution crack detection network incorporating se-
mantic guidance; its HrSegNet-B32 variant achieves real-time inference
while preserving fine crack details. Most recently, CarNet (Li et al.,
2024) introduced an olive-shaped encoder and a lightweight multiscale
decoder to improve detection performance and computational
efficiency.
2.2. Full-resolution segmentation networks
Recent studies (Pelt and Sethian, 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Yu and
Koltun, 2016) have shown that CNNs without downsampling layers can
effectively capture semantic information for segmentation tasks. Yu and
Koltun (2016) introduced dilated convolutions to aggregate multiscale
contextual information while preserving resolution. Varying dilation
rates allow feature capture at multiple scales, but their model suffers
from grid artifacts (Wang et al., 2018). To alleviate these gridding ar-
tifacts, Hamaguchi et al. (2018) proposed a local feature extraction
(LFE) network with dilation rates that increase and then decrease,
yielding strong results in remote sensing imagery. However, the
cascading atrous layers in this approach may struggle with long, narrow
objects like cracks. Pelt and Sethian (2018) developed a mixed-scale
dense network that combines dense connectivity with multiscale
feature extraction, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness in
image analysis.
In crack detection, few studies have focused on segmentation net-
works without downsampling. An early instance is CrackNet (Zhang
et al., 2017), which aims for pixel-level accuracy by merging convolu-
tional outputs with fully connected layers, but these layers are
parameter-heavy and computationally intensive. CrackNet-V (Fei et al.
2020) improved this by replacing the fully connected layers with 3 × 3
convolutions and deepened the network. Despite this improvement, the
authors noted that small filters across layers struggled to represent a
large receptive field, resulting in a loss of spatial information in wide
cracks. HACNet (Chen and Lin, 2021) utilizes atrous convolutions with
exponentially increasing dilation rates to expand the receptive field and
a hybrid connection to aggregate multi-level features. Although these
approaches achieve high accuracy, they increase computational de-
mands and latency, making real-time performance a challenge for full-
resolution architectures.
2.3. Attention modules in crack detection
Attention mechanisms have become a key component of modern
deep learning, helping models focus on relevant features while ignoring
irrelevant data. Inspired by their success in general vision tasks,
attention-based methods have been adapted for crack detection (Ranyal
et al., 2024). Liu et al. (2019) incorporated the SE attention module (Hu
et al., 2018) to optimize multi-dilation features. Wang et al. (2024) used
a coordinate attention module (Hou et al., 2021) to enhance the model's
perception of various spatial information. Qu and Wang (2023) intro-
duced the gating attention unit (Oktay, 2018) to reduce background
noise and improve crack localization. Tiny-Crack-Net (Chu et al., 2022)
explores the use of channel and spatial attention modules (Woo et al.,
2018) to capture spatial relationships and contextual information for
crack detection. CrackFormer (Liu et al., 2023) is a transformer-based
encoder-decoder structure that uses a combination of multiple local
self-attention modules and scaling-attention modules to capture fine-
grained crack features.
However, crack detection differs significantly from natural image
tasks (Chen et al., 2021). Cracks typically occupy a small portion of the
image, unlike natural scenes where objects, textures, and features are
more evenly distributed across the frame. Considering these distinctions,
we rethink the channel attention mechanism in this work and propose a
crack-aware attention module specifically tailored to the unique char-
acteristics of crack images.
3. Proposed approach
3.1. Network architecture
3.1.1. Revisiting HACNet
HACNet is a fully convolutional neural network designed to maintain
full-resolution throughout its structure, ensuring fine-grained spatial
information for crack segmentation. It comprises an input layer, two
HybridASPPs, and an output head, sequentially. HybridASPP is a block
of hybrid connected atrous convolutional layers that has a large recep-
tive field. The output head consolidates the outputs from the Hybrid-
ASPPs to generate the final prediction map. HACNet has the advantages
of a simple structure and fewer parameters but does not adequately
address computational inefficiency and limited feature representation.
The reasons are as follows: (1) performing all convolution operations on
full-resolution features results in high computational cost; (2) HACNet
lacks the ability to effectively model channel-wise feature dependencies,
which compromises discriminative feature representation.

3. Proposed approach
3.1. Network architecture
3.1.1. Revisiting HACNet
HACNet is a fully convolutional neural network designed to maintain
full-resolution throughout its structure, ensuring fine-grained spatial
information for crack segmentation. It comprises an input layer, two
HybridASPPs, and an output head, sequentially. HybridASPP is a block
of hybrid connected atrous convolutional layers that has a large recep-
tive field. The output head consolidates the outputs from the Hybrid-
ASPPs to generate the final prediction map. HACNet has the advantages
of a simple structure and fewer parameters but does not adequately
address computational inefficiency and limited feature representation.
The reasons are as follows: (1) performing all convolution operations on
full-resolution features results in high computational cost; (2) HACNet
lacks the ability to effectively model channel-wise feature dependencies,
which compromises discriminative feature representation.

3.4. Loss function
Since most pixels in the images are non-crack (background), we
adopt the same loss function as HACNet, combining binary cross-
entropy and Dice loss for training. For more details, please refer to the
HACNet paper (Chen & Lin, 2021). HACNetV2 has three side-output
layers and one fused prediction layer; as shown in Fig. 2. We imple-
ment a multi-layer supervision strategy (Lee et al., 2015); applying the
overall loss to each output individually. This enables more robust opti-
mization and ensures that the model can effectively handle the varied
outputs from the different branches.

The top portion of Table 4 focuses on lightweight, low-latency
models tested on the BCL and CHCrack5K datasets. Using only the
high-resolution branch, HACNetV2-HR achieves the best performance
among all the compared methods, including HrSegNetB32, Liu-

correlate with the actual inference speed (Ma et al., 2018). A model with
fewer FLOPS can exhibit higher inference latency due to inefficiencies in
memory usage, lack of hardware optimization, or architectural features
that hinder parallel execution.
Through inference efficiency analysis, we find that HACNetV2 is
highly scalable. The lightweight model HACNetV2-HR is compact and
efficient while maintaining competitive performance, making it well
suited for real-time applications. Moreover, HACNetV2, a medium-sized

effectiveness and efficiency of our network architecture. HACNetV2
processes 480 × 480 images at real-time speeds, achieving 47 FPS on a
single RTX 3090, which is slightly faster than HACNet-D, with improved
crack detection accuracy. By increasing the channel capacity to 48 in

and 0.24 % on CHCrack5K compared to the baseline HACNetV2. This
enhancement makes the model suitable for applications requiring high
detection accuracy, despite the increase in parameters and computa-

Despite its strengths, HACNetV2 encounters challenges when
detecting extremely fine cracks, particularly in images with complex
backgrounds. Fig. 9 (highlighted in yellow boxes) illustrates several
failure cases, where shallow cracks, thin cracks, and cracks against
intricate backgrounds (e.g., stains) are not accurately segmented. Red
boxes indicate false positives, such as over-segmentation errors
involving the edges of manhole covers and other structural elements.
These limitations may be due to the limited representation of such cases
in the training dataset, leading to an imbalance that impacts the learning
process. Furthermore, current deep learning models, including HAC-
NetV2, still face difficulties in generalizing to cracks of varying shapes
within complex backgrounds that have limited visual cues. We believe

5. Conclusions and future work
Automatic pixel-level crack detection is an essential task in the field
of infrastructure health monitoring. This study presents HACNetV2, a
scalable and efficient high-resolution architecture designed for precise
pixel-level crack detection. HACNetV2 achieves superior performance
on the BCL and CHCrack5K benchmark datasets while maintaining low
parameters and minimal computational cost. The key conclusions of this
study are as follows: (1) Even without the use of downsampling and
upsampling, the combination of a hybrid connection of atrous con-
volutional layers with exponentially increasing dilation rates and
channel attention mechanisms effectively aggregates multiscale features
across different receptive fields. This design improves the segmentation
accuracy for cracks of various sizes. (2) The integration of full-resolution
and high-resolution branches enables HACNetV2 to balance efficiency
and performance. This structure not only retains the advantage of pre-
serving more spatial detail but also benefits from strong representation
learning. (3) CrackAM improves the model's sensitivity to subtle crack
features, addressing the limitations of conventional attention
mechanisms that may overlook sparse crack details. (4) Different crack
detection scenarios impose varying requirements for detection accuracy
and computational efficiency. The flexible architecture of HACNetV2
allows for easy parameter adjustments to meet these diverse real-world
demands. We hope these insights contribute to advancements in other
defect tasks that require detailed spatial information.
